slides.title: Talking to software
bullets: Voice is the fastest input we have
Agents now answer in under a second
slides.notes: Voice agents feel natural because speaking is faster than typing. Modern pipelines respond in well under a second, which is the threshold where a conversation stops feeling like a form.
slides.narration: Let's start with why voice matters. Speaking is the fastest way we have to ask for something, and today's agents can answer in under a second. Over the next few slides I'll show you how that works.

slides.title: The cascaded pipeline
bullets: An LLM decides what to say
slides.notes: A cascaded pipeline has three stages: speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech. Each stage can be swapped, measured, and costed on its own, which is why I chose it over a single speech-to-speech model.
slides.narration: Most voice agents are built as a cascade. Speech-to-text turns your audio into words, a language model decides what to say, and text-to-speech speaks it back. Each stage can be swapped and measured on its own.

slides.title: Knowing when you speak
bullets: Voice activity detection runs in the browser
250 ms of speech confirms a real turn
Echo cancellation ignores the agent's voice
slides.notes: Voice activity detection runs locally in your browser and watches the microphone. Once it hears about a quarter second of continuous speech, it treats that as a real turn, and echo cancellation stops the agent from hearing itself.
slides.narration: To have a conversation, the agent has to know when you're talking. A small voice activity model runs right in the browser, waits for about a quarter second of real speech, and ignores the agent's own voice.

slides.title: Interrupting the agent
bullets: Playback stops the instant you speak
Only words you heard stay in memory
slides.notes: When you interrupt, playback stops immediately, every in-flight request is aborted, and the conversation history keeps only the sentences you actually heard. That way the agent never assumes it said something you missed.
slides.narration: You can cut me off at any time. The moment you speak, playback stops, pending requests are cancelled, and I only remember the words you actually heard.

slides.title: Where latency comes from
slides.notes: Most of the delay comes from three places: transcription, the first token from the language model, and the first audio from text-to-speech. Streaming each sentence to speech as soon as it's written hides most of it.
slides.narration: Here's where the time goes. Transcription, the first token from the model, and the first audio byte each add a few hundred milliseconds. Streaming sentence by sentence hides most of it.

slides.title: Running it for free
bullets: Free tiers for speech, LLM, and hosting
Automatic fallback when a quota runs out
Every token is counted and shown
slides.notes: Everything here runs on free tiers. When a provider hits its rate limit, the system falls back to another one automatically, and every token is counted so the cost is always visible.
slides.narration: Finally, cost. This whole system runs on free tiers, falls back automatically when a quota runs out, and counts every token so you can see exactly what each answer costs.
